facts.text: Arab–Byzantine wars: Led by Ibrahim II of Ifriqiya, Aghlabid forces captured the Byzantine stronghold of Taormina, concluding the Muslim conquest of Sicily.
George Louis, Elector of Hanover, became King George I of Great Britain, marking the beginning of the Georgian era.
British scientist Joseph Priestley liberated oxygen gas, corroborating the discovery of the element by the German-Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele.

French Revolutionary Wars: The Battle of the Nile, between a British fleet commanded by Horatio Nelson and a French fleet under François-Paul Brueys d'Aigalliers, began at Aboukir Bay off the Egyptian coast.
First Barbary War: USS Enterprise, an American schooner, captured the Tripolitan polacca Tripoli in a single-ship action off the coast of Libya.
Three days of rioting erupted after a parade in Philadelphia, celebrating the end of slavery in the West Indies, was attacked by a mob.

links.title: Slavery in the British and French Caribbean

facts.text: Colorado was admitted as the 38th U.S. state.
Jef Denyn hosted the world's first carillon concert at St. Rumbold's Cathedral in Mechelen, Belgium.
Harriet Quimby became the first woman to earn an Aero Club of America aviator certificate.
Several days of anti-Jewish rioting began in Bratislava, instigated by former Slovak partisans opposed to the restitution of Jewish property after the Holocaust in Slovakia.
" Video Killed the Radio Star " by the Buggles became the first music video broadcast on the American cable television network MTV.

links.title: List of first music videos aired on MTV

facts.text: Commercial peat cutters discovered a preserved bog body, now known as Lindow Man, at Lindow Moss in Cheshire, England.

image.caption: Died Between 2 BC and 119 AD Lindow Moss, Cheshire, England

facts.text: U.S. president George H. W. Bush delivered a speech in the Ukrainian parliament in Kiev warning against independence from the Soviet Union.
A shooting at a branch of the Israeli LGBT organization the Aguda in Tel Aviv resulted in two deaths.

links.title: The Aguda - The Association for LGBTQ Equality in Israel

facts.text: Upon the death of Justin I, his nephew and adopted son Justinian I became the sole ruler of the Byzantine Empire.
Britain celebrated a Grand Jubilee to mark 100 years since the accession of George I and 16 years since the start of the Battle of the Nile.
The Concert for Bangladesh, a pair of benefit concerts organised by George Harrison and Ravi Shankar for refugees of the Bangladesh genocide, took place at Madison Square Garden in New York.
Nearly 400 people died in a supermarket fire in Asunción, Paraguay, when exits were locked to prevent people from stealing merchandise.
Bridge 9340, carrying Interstate 35W across the Mississippi River in Minneapolis, United States, suffered a catastrophic failure and collapsed, killing 13 people and injuring 145 others.
Unpopular among the Senate aristocracy for his reforming efforts, Roman emperor Majorian was deposed by Ricimer and executed five days later.
While on a hunting trip in the New Forest, King William II of England was killed by an arrow through the lung loosed by one of his own men.
The first United States census was officially completed, with the nation's residential population enumerated to be 3,929,214.
The French army's general headquarters was activated in anticipation of war with Germany.
An explosion, blamed on Austro-Hungarian saboteurs, sank the Italian dreadnought Leonardo da Vinci.
Nepalese author Krishna Lal Adhikari was sentenced to nine years in prison for publishing a book about the cultivation of corn alleged to contain attacks on the ruling dynasty.

Leo Szilard penned a letter, signed by Albert Einstein and addressed to U.S. president Franklin D. Roosevelt, warning that Germany may develop atomic bombs, leading to the establishment of the Manhattan Project.
Star Dust, a British South American Airways airliner, crashed into Mount Tupungato in the Argentine Andes; its wreckage was not found until 1998.

links.title: 1947 BSAA Avro Lancastrian Star Dust accident

facts.text: A flash fire killed 50 people at a leisure centre in Douglas, Isle of Man.
One of the world's earliest underground tube railways opened in the Tower Subway (interior depicted), a tunnel beneath the River Thames in London.
Calvin Coolidge became the 30th president of the United States after Warren G. Harding suffered a fatal heart attack.

At the California Institute of Technology, American physicist Carl David Anderson proved the existence of antimatter with the discovery of the positron, for which he would receive the 1936 Nobel Prize in Physics.
The English rock band the Who released Who's Next, their only album to top the UK charts.
Raúl Iturriaga, a former deputy director of the Chilean secret police, was captured in Viña del Mar after having been on the run following a kidnapping conviction.
Pope Stephen IX was crowned as pope.
Hundred Years' War: The French town of Calais capitulated to English forces after an eleven-month siege, ending the Crécy campaign.
Macedonian rebels in Kruševo proclaimed a republic, which existed for ten days before Ottoman forces destroyed the town.
Jiddu Krishnamurti, believed by some Theosophists to be a likely candidate for the messianic " World Teacher ", dissolved the Order of the Star, the organisation established to support him.

links.title: Order of the Star in the East

facts.text: African-American athlete Jesse Owens won the first of his four gold medals at the Berlin Olympics, dashing Nazi leaders' hopes of Aryan domination at the games.
Fighting Dinosaurs, a fossil specimen featuring a Velociraptor and a Protoceratops in combat, was unearthed in the Djadochta Formation of Mongolia.
Tandy Corporation announced the TRS-80, one of the world's first mass-produced personal computers.
The Sky Tower, then the tallest free-standing structure in the Southern Hemisphere at 328 m (1,076 ft), opened in Auckland, New Zealand.

links.title: List of tallest buildings and structures

facts.text: Mauritanian president Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya was overthrown in a military coup while he attended the funeral of King Fahd of Saudi Arabia.
Indian Rebellion: An eight-day siege of a fortified outbuilding in Arrah occupied by 68 defenders against more than 10,000 men ended when a relief party dispersed the besiegers.
An agricultural workers' strike in Wheatland degenerated into a riot, becoming one of the first major farm-labor confrontations in California.
World War II: Italian forces began a conquest of British Somaliland, capturing the region in 16 days.
A privately chartered Boeing 707 struck a mountain peak and crashed near Agadir, Morocco, killing 188.

links.title: 1975 Agadir Royal Air Maroc Boeing 707 crash

facts.text: The last vessels involved in Taurus 09, a Royal Navy training deployment covering 20,400 miles (32,800 km), returned to HMNB Devonport, England.
Hundred Years' War: A large-scale mounted raid by Anglo-Gascon forces began under the command of Edward the Black Prince.
War of the Spanish Succession: A combined Anglo-Dutch fleet under the command of George Rooke and allied with Archduke Charles captured Gibraltar from Spain.
Mount Asama in Japan began a climactic eruption, which exacerbated the Great Tenmei famine and led to thousands of deaths.
The signing of the Treaty of Sistova brought an end to the Austro-Turkish War.
French Revolutionary Wars: Commanded by Napoleon Bonaparte (depicted), the French Army of Italy decisively defeated Austrian forces led by Peter Vitus von Quosdanovich at the Battle of Lonato.
American surveyor James Thompson produced the first plat of Chicago for the Illinois and Michigan Canal Commissioners.
Lizzie Borden 's father and stepmother were found murdered in their home in Fall River, Massachusetts; Borden was later tried and acquitted for the murders.
World War I: Adhering to the terms of the Treaty of London, the United Kingdom declared war on Germany in response to the latter's invasion of Belgium.
Alfred C. Glassell Jr. caught a black marlin weighing 1,560 lb (710 kg) off the coast of Peru, setting the record for the largest bony fish caught by hand.

Vietnam War: The National Security Agency falsely claimed that a U.S. Navy destroyer was attacked a second time by North Vietnamese vessels in the Gulf of Tonkin, leading Congress to authorize the use of military force.
President Idi Amin announced the expulsion of Asians from Uganda.
Jean-Baptiste Ouédraogo, the president of Upper Volta, was ousted in a coup d'état led by Thomas Sankara.
Yugoslav Wars: The Croatian Army initiated Operation Storm, the last major battle of the Croatian War of Independence and the largest European land battle since the Second World War.
French supercentenarian Jeanne Calment died at the age of 122 years, 164 days, with the longest confirmed human lifespan in history.

An airport police officer discovered a suitcase containing approximately US$800,000 as it passed through security at Jorge Newbery Airfield in Buenos Aires, sparking an international scandal involving Venezuela and Argentina.
Julieka Ivanna Dhu, an Aboriginal Australian woman, died in police custody after her deteriorating condition was mocked and ignored.
Second Barons' War: Royal troops led by Prince Edward defeated baronial forces under Simon de Montfort at the Battle of Evesham in Worcestershire, England.

links.title: Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester

facts.text: In Brooklyn, a mob composed largely of Irish Americans attacked a group of African Americans in a riot.
An explosion on the Greek cruise ship MTS Oceanos ruptured its hull, causing it to sink off the east coast of South Africa, with all 571 people on board rescued.
Sri Lankan civil war: Seventeen employees of the French nongovernmental organization ACF International were massacred in Mutur.
A large explosion of ammonium nitrate stored at the Port of Beirut in Lebanon killed 218 people and caused US$15 billion in damage.
Henry I was crowned King of England in Westminster Abbey.
The Kingdom of Scotland captures Roxburgh, one of the last English strongholds in Scotland, following a siege.
Beaver Wars: Aggravated by increased French incursions into their territory, a large force of Mohawk warriors substantially destroyed the settlement of Lachine in present-day Quebec.
Austro-Turkish War: The Ottoman army were defeated in their attempt to capture the Habsburgs -controlled Petrovaradin Fortress despite having double the number of soldiers.
Sir John Barrow, secretary at the Admiralty, rejected a proposal to use Francis Ronalds 's electrical telegraph, deeming it "wholly unnecessary".
Bertha Benz made the first long-distance automobile trip, driving 106 km (66 mi) from Mannheim to Pforzheim, Germany, in a Benz Patent-Motorwagen.
First World War: The British Empire's Sinai and Palestine campaign began with a victory at the Battle of Romani.
An earthquake registering 6.4 M s struck near Ambato, Ecuador, killing 5,050 people.
American actress and model Marilyn Monroe was found dead of a barbiturate overdose in her home in Brentwood, Los Angeles.
Police raided a screening of the film Lonesome Cowboys in Atlanta, Georgia, leading to the creation of a Gay Liberation Front in that city.
U.S. president Ronald Reagan fired the 11,345 striking members of the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization en masse.
A Biman Bangladesh Airlines aircraft crashed while attempting to land in Dhaka, killing 49 people in the deadliest aviation accident in Bangladeshi history.

links.title: 1984 Biman Bangladesh Airlines Fokker F27 crash

facts.text: Wizards of the Coast released Magic: The Gathering, the first trading card game.
NASA launched the Juno probe to Jupiter as part of the New Frontiers program.
Radio Network House, damaged in the 2011 Christchurch earthquake, becomes the first building to be demolished by implosion in New Zealand.
An American white supremacist carried out a mass shooting at a Sikh temple in Oak Creek, Wisconsin, killing six people and wounding four others.
A python killed two boys in Campbellton, New Brunswick, Canada.
Muscovite–Lithuanian Wars: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania achieved one of the greatest Lithuanian victories against the Tatars at the Battle of Kletsk.
Scottish nobleman John Ruthven, 3rd Earl of Gowrie, was killed during what was most likely a failed attempt to kidnap King James VI.
Russia, Prussia and Habsburg Austria began the First Partition of Poland, with the primary motive to restore the regional balance of power in Eastern Europe.
Due to an athletics scandal, the National Collegiate Athletic Association applied the death penalty to the basketball program at the University of Southwestern Louisiana.

links.title: University of Southwestern Louisiana basketball scandal

facts.text: United States Environmental Protection Agency personnel accidentally caused a spillage of 3 million gallons (11 million litres) of mine waste water and tailings trapped inside the Gold King Mine near Silverton, Colorado.

links.title: 2015 Gold King Mine waste water spill

facts.text: Second Fitna: Pro- Alid forces defeated the Umayyad Caliphate in the Battle of Khazir, allowing them to take control of Mosul in present-day Iraq.
After the death of Gregory XV, a papal conclave in Rome elected Maffeo Barberini as Pope Urban VIII.
The Anglo-Belgian India Rubber Company was founded in Antwerp to exploit natural rubber in the Congo Free State.
New York Supreme Court judge Joseph Force Crater disappeared in Manhattan, in a case that was never solved.
World War II: Allied forces attacked German fortifications at Saint-Malo, France, beginning the Battle of Saint-Malo.

image.caption: Date 4 August – 2 September 1944 Location Saint-Malo , France 48°38′14″N 2°01′45″W ﻿ / ﻿ 48.6372°N 2.0292°W ﻿ / 48.6372; -2.0292 Result Allied victory

facts.text: An earthquake struck along the Calaveras Fault near Coyote Lake, California, injuring sixteen people.
Researchers announced that the meteorite ALH84001, discovered in the Allan Hills of Antarctica, may contain evidence of life on Mars, but further tests were inconclusive.
Korean Air Flight 801 crashed into a hill on approach to Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport in Guam, killing 228 of the 254 people aboard.

links.title: Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport

facts.text: Flash floods, mudslides, and debris flows across the Ladakh region of Indian-administered Kashmir left at least 255 people dead.
A series of riots broke out in several London boroughs and in cities and towns across England in response to the shooting of Mark Duggan by Metropolitan Police officers.
A gas leak caused an explosion that collapsed a building and led to the deaths of 22 people in Rosario, Argentina.
The Battle of Oriskany, one of the bloodiest battles of the American Revolutionary War, was fought about 6 mi (10 km) east of Fort Stanwix, New York.
World War II: The U.S. Army Air Force bomber Enola Gay dropped the Little Boy atomic bomb on Hiroshima, Japan, killing about 70,000 people instantly.

links.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

facts.text: U.S. president Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act into law, outlawing literacy tests and other discriminatory voting practices that had been responsible for the widespread disfranchisement of African Americans.
British computer programmer Tim Berners-Lee posted a public invitation to collaborate on a system of interlinked, hypertext documents accessible via the Internet, known as the World Wide Web.
Mauritanian president Sidi Ould Cheikh Abdallahi was ousted from power by a group of high-ranking generals that he had dismissed from office several hours earlier.
Prussia declared its intervention in the War of the Austrian Succession on behalf of Charles VII, beginning the Second Silesian War.
The Badge of Military Merit, the precursor to the U.S. Purple Heart, was established as a military decoration of the Continental Army.
The first section of the Great Northern Railway, now the southern section of the East Coast Main Line, opened between London and Peterborough.
Mahdist War: Anglo-Egyptian soldiers clashed with Mahdist Sudanese rebels in the Battle of Abu Hamed.
Fifty-nine days after leaving New York City with three passengers, Alice Huyler Ramsey arrived in San Francisco to become the first woman to drive an automobile across the contiguous United States.
The Battle of Mulhouse began with France's first attack of World War I in an ultimately unsuccessful attempt to recover the region of Alsace from Germany.
IBM presented the first program-controlled calculator to Harvard University, after which it became known as the Mark I.

image.caption: Also known as IBM Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator (ASCC)

facts.text: Hurricane Diane, the first Atlantic hurricane to cause more than $1 billion in damages, formed between the Lesser Antilles and Cape Verde.
Lynne Cox became the first person to swim between the U.S. and the Soviet Union, crossing from Little Diomede to Big Diomede in the Bering Strait in 2 hours and 5 minutes.

Car bombs exploded simultaneously at the American embassies in the East African capital cities of Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, and Nairobi, Kenya, killing more than 200 people and injuring more than 4,000 others.

links.title: List of diplomatic missions of the United States

facts.text: Ming Chinese general Cao Qin staged a failed coup against the Tianshun Emperor.
World War II: U.S. Marines initiated the first American offensive of the Guadalcanal campaign, with landings on Tulagi, Gavutu – Tanambogo and Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands.

image.caption: Date 7–9 August 1942 Location Tulagi and Gavutu in the Solomon Islands 9°07′S 160°10′E ﻿ / ﻿ 9.11°S 160.17°E ﻿ / -9.11; 160.17 Result Allied victory

facts.text: The Soviet Union informed Turkey that the way in which the latter was handling the Turkish straits no longer represented the security interests of its fellow Black Sea nations, escalating the Turkish Straits crisis.
Jonathan Jackson took hostages in a courthouse in Marin County, California, to coerce the release of the Soledad Brothers, resulting in the deaths of judge Harold Haley and three others.
Five members of the Bamber family were found murdered at a farmhouse in Tolleshunt D'Arcy, England.
Reconquista: In the early stages of the Mudéjar revolt, Muslim rebels captured the Alcázar of Jerez de la Frontera in present-day Spain, holding it for about two months.

links.title: Alcázar of Jerez de la Frontera

facts.text: The cornerstone of Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe 's observatory Uraniborg was laid on the island of Hven.
The Third Anglo-Afghan War ended with the United Kingdom signing a treaty to recognise the independence of the Emirate of Afghanistan.
The Endurance departed Plymouth, England, on the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition.
The German airship Graf Zeppelin departed Lakehurst, New Jersey, on a flight to circumnavigate the world.
At a zebra crossing on Abbey Road in London, Iain Macmillan took the photograph that was used for the cover of the Beatles ' album Abbey Road.
A mining disaster killed 262 workers, mainly Italian nationals, at the Bois du Cazier coal mine in Belgium.
At a zebra crossing in London, photographer Iain Macmillan took the photo that was used for the cover of the Beatles ' album Abbey Road.
Tropical Storm Beryl formed over southeastern Louisiana, making it one of the few tropical cyclones to form over land.
A series of marches, demonstrations, protests, and riots, which became known as the 8888 Uprising, began against the one-party state of the Burma Socialist Programme Party.
Hudson Volcano in Chile began to erupt, depositing volcanic ash over 150,000 square kilometres (58,000 sq mi).
The Iranian consulate in Mazar-i-Sharif, Afghanistan, was raided by Taliban leading to the death of 10 Iranian diplomats and an Iranian journalist.

links.title: 1998 killing of Iranian diplomats in Afghanistan

facts.text: A EuroCity train en route to Prague struck a part of a motorway bridge that had fallen onto the track near Studénka station and derailed, killing 8 people and injuring 64 others.
Nine people died when a tour helicopter and a small private airplane collided over the Hudson River in Hoboken, New Jersey.
The World Health Organization declared the Western African Ebola epidemic, which began in December 2013, to be a public health emergency of international concern.

links.title: Public health emergency of international concern

facts.text: The foundation for what is now known as the Wren Building, the oldest surviving college building in the United States, was laid in a ceremony at Middle Plantation, Virginia.
The Battle of Amiens began in northern France, marking the start of the Allies ' Hundred Days Offensive through the German front lines that ultimately led to the end of World War I.
The Warsaw radio mast, then the tallest structure ever built, at 646.38 metres (2,120.7 ft), collapsed due to an error in exchanging the guys on the highest telecommunications equipment of the mast.

image.caption: Interactive map of the Warsaw radio mast area

facts.text: A massive mudslide in the Chinese province of Gansu killed at least 1,471 people.
The statue of A'a from Rurutu was presented to members of the London Missionary Society on the south Pacific island of Ra'iatea.
Nez Perce War: Both the Nez Perce and the United States Army suffered numerous casualties at the Battle of the Big Hole, which ended conclusively.
The first meeting of the International Congress of Mathematicians was held in Zürich, Switzerland.
The Blue Lotus, the fifth volume of The Adventures of Tintin by the Belgian cartoonist Hergé and noted for its emphasis on countering negative misconceptions of Chinese people, began serialisation.
World War II: In the first major naval engagement of the Guadalcanal campaign, Japan forced the U.S. Navy to withdraw from the Solomon Islands.
Shostakovich's Symphony No. 7 was premiered in Leningrad while the city was under siege by Nazi forces.

links.title: Leningrad première of Shostakovich's Symphony No. 7

facts.text: The United States Forest Service authorized the use of Smokey Bear as its mascot to replace Bambi.
World War II: The USAAF bomber Bockscar dropped a Fat Man atomic bomb on Nagasaki, Japan.

links.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

facts.text: About 20,000 women marched on Pretoria, South Africa, to protest the introduction of pass laws for black women under apartheid.
Led by Albert Kalonji, South Kasai declared its unilateral secession from the Republic of the Congo (Léopoldville).
Members of the Manson Family invaded a house and murdered American actress Sharon Tate and four guests in Los Angeles, before killing two more people the following night.
The Troubles: British forces began arresting and interning suspected Irish republican militants in Northern Ireland.
On the verge of an impeachment and removal from office amid the Watergate scandal, Richard Nixon became the first president of the United States to resign.
Wayne Gretzky was traded from the Edmonton Oilers to the Los Angeles Kings in one of the most controversial player transactions in ice hockey history.
A civilian school bus in Dahyan, Yemen, was bombed by Saudi Arabia killing at least 40 children under 15.
Michael Brown, an 18-year-old African-American man, was killed by a white police officer in Ferguson, Missouri, resulting in widespread protests and unrest.
A civilian school bus in Dahyan, Yemen, was bombed by Saudi Arabia, killing at least 40 children under 15.
American Civil War: Confederate troops counter-attacked and won the Battle of Cedar Mountain, after nearly being driven from the field in the early part of the battle.
In a ceremony at Westminster Abbey, Edward VII and Alexandra were crowned King and Queen of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, and Emperor and Empress of India.

links.title: Coronation of Edward VII and Alexandra

facts.text: The state of Singapore was expelled from the Malaysian federation due to a heated ideological conflict between their ruling parties; the day is now celebrated as Singapore's National Day.

links.title: History of the Republic of Singapore

facts.text: Second Intifada: A suicide bomber attacked a pizza restaurant in Jerusalem, killing 15 people and wounding 130 others.
British police arrested 24 people for conspiring to detonate liquid explosives carried on board airliners travelling from the UK to the US and Canada.
The Swedish warship Vasa sank shortly after departing Stockholm on her maiden voyage to take part in the Thirty Years' War.
The first wave of the Expulsion of the Acadians from the present-day Canadian Maritime provinces by the British began with the Bay of Fundy campaign at Chignecto.
French Revolution: Insurrectionists in Paris stormed the Tuileries Palace (depicted), effectively ending the French monarchy until it was restored in 1814.
The Louvre in Paris, today the world's most-visited museum, opened with an exhibition of 537 paintings and 184 objets d'art.
From measurements of its motion, German astronomer Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel deduced that Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, had an unseen companion.
American Civil War: The first major battle west of the Mississippi River, the Battle of Wilson's Creek, was fought.
José Antônio Saraiva announced that the Brazilian military would exact reprisals after Uruguay's governing Blanco Party refused Brazil's demands, beginning the Uruguayan War.
The Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers began an ultimately unsuccessful strike to reverse its declining fortunes and organize large numbers of new members.

links.title: Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers

facts.text: First Indochina War: The French Union withdrew its forces from Operation Camargue against the Việt Minh in central modern-day Vietnam.
The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 became law, authorizing reparations to surviving Japanese Americans interned during World War II.
Having already caused severe flooding in the Philippines, Typhoon Lekima made landfall in Zhejiang, China, killing 45 people in the province.

Hungarian invasions of Europe: Forces under Otto the Great were victorious at the Battle of Lechfeld (depicted) near present-day Augsburg, Germany, holding off the incursions of the Magyars into Central Europe.
Yekuno Amlak deposed the last Zagwe king and seized the imperial throne of Ethiopia, beginning the reign of the Solomonic dynasty, which would last for more than 700 years.
The Heron Road Bridge in Ottawa, Canada, collapsed during its construction, killing nine workers.
Amid large protests against the impending demolition of the Queen's Pier, the High Court of Hong Kong dismissed legal attempts to preserve the landmark.
Jeffrey Epstein, an American financier and convicted sex offender, was found dead in his cell at the Metropolitan Correctional Center, New York.
Reconquista: Aragonese forces led by King James II landed on the coast of Almería, beginning an ultimately unsuccessful siege of the city, then held by the Emirate of Granada.
The first conclave to be held in the Sistine Chapel elected Roderic Borja as Pope Alexander VI to succeed Innocent VIII.
Francis Light founded George Town, the first British settlement in Southeast Asia and the present-day capital of the Malaysian state of Penang.
The first Bud Billiken Parade and Picnic, the oldest and largest African-American parade in the United States, was held in Chicago.
Amid rumors of kidnappings of children by Jews in Kraków, a crowd of Poles took part in a pogrom, resulting in at least one death.
At a party in New York City, Jamaican musician DJ Kool Herc began rapping during an extended break, laying the foundation for hip hop music.
Two Aeroflot passenger jets collided in mid-air near Dniprodzerzhynsk in the Ukrainian SSR, killing all 178 people on both aircraft.
Ken Levine 's System Shock 2 was released to mediocre sales, but later received critical acclaim and influenced subsequent first-person shooter game design.
At least 306 people were killed and 3,000 others injured in a pair of earthquakes near Tabriz, Iran.
The region of Dacia, comprising parts of modern Romania, became a province of the Roman Empire.
King Talal of Jordan was forced to abdicate due to mental illness and was succeeded by his eldest son Hussein.
The Timorese Democratic Union launched a coup in Portuguese Timor, starting the East Timorese civil war.
The U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration initiated an investigation into the alleged vulnerability of the Ford Pinto to fuel leakage and fire in a rear-end collision.
A tornado struck downtown Salt Lake City, damaging 120 homes and injuring over 100 people.
Crusades: Fatimid forces under al-Afdal Shahanshah began retreating to Egypt after the Battle of Ascalon, concluding the First Crusade.
A race riot in Philadelphia destroyed African-American businesses and killed two people.
The last known quagga, a subspecies of the plains zebra, died at Natura Artis Magistra, a zoo in Amsterdam.

image.caption: A quagga mare at the London Zoo in 1870, one of two specimens photographed alive

facts.text: World War I: Belgian troops won a victory at the Battle of Halen, but were ultimately unable to stop the German invasion of Belgium.
World War II: In Sant'Anna di Stazzema, Italy, the Waffen-SS and the Brigate Nere murdered about 560 local villagers and refugees and burned their bodies.
An official administrative history of the Manhattan Project, written by American physicist Henry DeWolf Smyth, was released to the public days after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

links.title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

facts.text: The Troubles: Riots erupted in the neighbourhood of Bogside in Derry, and spread across much of Northern Ireland.
Near Faith, South Dakota, American paleontologist Sue Hendrickson found one of the most complete Tyrannosaurus rex skeletons, nicknamed Sue.
Franco-American children as young as seven years old began striking against Cabot Mill in Brunswick, Maine, shutting down operations for three days.
Thirteen Jewish poets were executed in Moscow for espionage based on false confessions.

Japan Air Lines Flight 123 crashed into Mount Takamagahara in Gunma Prefecture, killing 520 of 524 people on board, including singer Kyu Sakamoto, in the world's worst single-aircraft aviation disaster.
Kursk, an Oscar-class submarine of the Russian Navy, suffered an on-board explosion and sank in the Barents Sea during a military exercise, killing 118 people.
The state-owned Taedonggang Brewing Company inaugurated the first beer festival in North Korea.
War of the Spanish Succession: The Duke of Marlborough led Allied forces to a crucial victory at the Battle of Blenheim.
Bach led the Thomanerchor in Leipzig in the first performance of the chorale cantata, Nimm von uns, Herr, du treuer Gott, BWV 101.

links.title: Nimm von uns, Herr, du treuer Gott, BWV 101

facts.text: Anglo-Spanish War: The United Kingdom captured Havana after a five-week siege, holding it until the Treaty of Paris the following year.
A major earthquake near Arica, Peru (now in Chile), caused an estimated 25,000 casualties; the subsequent tsunami caused considerable damage as far away as Hawaii and New Zealand.
The first Bayreuth Festival, created by Richard Wagner and his wife Cosima to showcase his stage works, was opened with Das Rheingold.
Members of the U.S. Army's all-black 25th Infantry Regiment were accused of killing a white bartender and wounding a white police officer in Brownsville, Texas, despite exculpatory evidence.
The Act on National Flag and Anthem was adopted, formally establishing the Hinomaru and " Kimigayo " as the Japanese national flag and anthem, respectively.

links.title: Act on National Flag and Anthem

facts.text: Merely 22 hours after Tropical Storm Bonnie struck the U.S. state of Florida, Hurricane Charley inflicted further damage to the region.
Maurice was crowned Byzantine emperor to succeed Tiberius II Constantine.
General George Monck founded the predecessor to the Coldstream Guards, the oldest regular regiment of the British Army in continuous active service.
Opha May Johnson became the first woman to enlist in the United States Marine Corps.

image.caption: Born Opha May Jacob ( 1878-05-04 ) May 4, 1878 Kokomo, Indiana , U.S.

facts.text: World War II: The German Luftwaffe launched an air operation, codenamed Adlertag, to destroy the British Royal Air Force; its failure indefinitely postponed the German invasion of the United Kingdom.
After being boarded by Canadian authorities, MV Sun Sea docked in British Columbia and the 492 Sri Lankan Tamil refugee claimants on board were placed into detention.
War of Saint Sabas: A Genoese fleet captured or sank most of the ships of a Venetian trade convoy off the Albanian coast.
The United Kingdom formally annexed the Tristan da Cunha archipelago, administering the islands from the Cape Colony in South Africa.

After a secret meeting in Newfoundland, British prime minister Winston Churchill and U.S. president Franklin D. Roosevelt issued the Atlantic Charter, establishing a vision for a post–World War II world.
The inaugural edition of the Youth Olympic Games opened in Singapore for athletes aged between 14 and 18.
Security forces raided two camps of supporters of the ousted Egyptian president Mohamed Morsi in Cairo, leading to the deaths of at least 595 civilians.
A magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck in Haiti, killing at least 2,248 people and causing $1.5 billion in damages and economic loss.
The Spanish Villasur expedition, intended to slow the progress of French influence on the Great Plains of North America, ended in failure when it was ambushed (depicted) by Pawnee and Otoe forces.
One of the first recordings of music, of Arthur Sullivan 's " The Lost Chord ", was played at a press conference in London to introduce Thomas Edison 's phonograph.
The Rocky Horror Picture Show premiered in London, the first in its record-breaking run in cinemas, which continues in limited release.
Helios Airways Flight 522 crashed into a mountain north of Marathon, Greece, killing all 121 people on board.
Four coordinated suicide bomb attacks detonated in the Yazidi communities of Qahtaniya and Jazeera, Iraq, killing 796 people and wounding 1,562 others.
Forces of the Umayyad Caliphate abandoned a year-long siege of Constantinople, ending their goal of conquering the Byzantine Empire.
Upon the death of his uncle Stephen I, Peter (depicted) became the second king of Hungary.
Michael VIII Palaiologos was crowned Byzantine emperor in Constantinople.
A military coup against the government of Dimitrios Rallis began in the neighbourhood of Goudi in Athens, Greece.
Josef Jakobs, a German spy, became the last person executed at the Tower of London.
World War II: The tanker SS Ohio reached Malta as part of an operation to deliver much-needed supplies during the siege of Malta.
World War II: Allied forces began Operation Dragoon, their invasion of southern France.
Jawaharlal Nehru took office as the first prime minister of India, a post he held for 16 years.
The Republic of Korea was established with Syngman Rhee as its first president.
Big Ear, a radio telescope at Ohio State University received a strong, apparently extraterrestrial radio signal that became known as the Wow! signal.
The Troubles: A car bomb attack carried out by the Real Irish Republican Army killed 29 people and injured approximately 220 others in Omagh, Northern Ireland.
Byzantine general Eustathios Daphnomeles captured and blinded Ibatzes of Bulgaria by means of a ruse, ending the last resistance against Emperor Basil II 's conquest of Bulgaria.
Byzantine–Ottoman wars: The Empire of Trebizond, the longest-surviving Byzantine successor state, was conquered by Ottoman forces following a month-long siege.
War of 1812: Potawatomi warriors ambushed a United States Army convoy after it had evacuated Fort Dearborn, in present-day Chicago, and razed the fort.

image.caption: Date August 15, 1812 Location Present-day Chicago , Illinois 41°51′28″N 87°37′9″W ﻿ / ﻿ 41.85778°N 87.61917°W ﻿ / 41.85778; -87.61917 Result Potawatomi victory

facts.text: President Fulbert Youlou was overthrown in the Republic of Congo, after a three-day uprising in the capital.
The Helsinki Agreement between the Free Aceh Movement and the Government of Indonesia was signed, ending more than 28 years of fighting.
American Revolutionary War: American forces routed British and German troops at the Battle of Bennington in Walloomsac, New York.
Around 15 people were killed and 400 to 700 others injured when cavalry charged into a crowd demanding the reform of parliamentary representation in Manchester, England.
Daaga and two other African soldiers in the British Army's 1st West India Regiment were executed for their role in the St. Joseph Mutiny in Trinidad.
San Sebastian Church, an all-iron church in Manila, was officially consecrated.
A group including George Carmack and Skookum Jim Mason discovered gold near Dawson City, Canada, setting off the Klondike Gold Rush.

image.caption: Other names Alaska Gold Rush, Yukon Gold Rush

facts.text: An earthquake registering approximately 8.2 M w struck Valparaíso, Chile, killing 3,882 people.
The Battle of Radzymin, one of the bloodiest and most intense battles of the Polish–Soviet War, concluded with a Polish victory.
Ray Chapman of the Cleveland Indians was hit by a pitch and died the following day, becoming the only Major League Baseball player to die directly as a result of injuries sustained during a game.
A long-running dispute between Muslims and Jews over access to the Western Wall in Jerusalem escalated into a week-long period of violent riots throughout Palestine.
The Holocaust: During the deportation of Jews from Slovakia, President Jozef Tiso gave a speech describing Jews as "parasites" and "the eternal enemy".

links.title: List of Holocaust transports from Slovakia

facts.text: The Stanley Internment Camp in Hong Kong was liberated following the announcement of the surrender of Japan in World War II.
Widespread riots between Hindus and Muslims took place in Calcutta following the All-India Muslim League 's call for an independent Pakistan.
The English rock band the Beatles fired their drummer Pete Best, replacing him with Ringo Starr.

image.caption: Born Richard Starkey ( 1940-07-07 ) 7 July 1940 (age 85) Liverpool , England

facts.text: Typhoon Wayne formed over the South China Sea, going on to become one of the longest-lived tropical cyclones in the north-western Pacific, lasting 21 days.
At the World Championships in Athletics in Berlin, Usain Bolt ran the 100 metres in 9.58 seconds, breaking his own record set a year earlier.
War of the League of Cambrai: English and Imperial forces defeated French cavalry, forcing them to retreat.

links.title: War of the League of Cambrai

facts.text: Second Boer War: A 10,000-strong column of soldiers led by Lord Kitchener broke a 13-day siege of a small garrison.
The British parliament's Blind Persons Act received royal assent.
American singer and actor Elvis Presley was found dead in his home in Memphis, Tennessee.

image.caption: Born Elvis Aaron Presley [ a ] ( 1935-01-08 ) January 8, 1935 Tupelo, Mississippi , US

facts.text: Suicide bombers assassinated Pakistani politician Shuja Khanzada and killed at least 21 others at his home in Attock District.
An earthquake struck the North Anatolia region, killing over 8,000 people.
Scanian War: Swedish forces defeated Danish troops at the Battle of Halmstad.
The premiere of Götterdämmerung by Richard Wagner closed the first Bayreuth Festival.

World War I: Ignoring orders to retreat, Hermann von François led a successful counterattack defending East Prussia at the Battle of Stallupönen and scored the first German victory in the Eastern Front.
A category 4 hurricane made landfall in Galveston, Texas, leaving at least 275 people dead and causing $50 million in damage.
Winston Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt met in a highly secret military conference held in Quebec City.
World War II: The Royal Air Force began a strategic bombing campaign against Nazi Germany's V-weapon programme by attacking the Peenemünde Army Research Center.

links.title: Strategic bombing during World War II

facts.text: The independence of Indonesia was proclaimed by Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta, igniting a revolution against the Dutch Empire.
Animal Farm, George Orwell 's satirical allegory of Soviet totalitarianism, was first published.
American musician Miles Davis released Kind of Blue, which became one of the best-selling and most critically acclaimed jazz recordings of all time.
Byzantine–Bulgarian wars: The Bulgarians defeated Byzantine forces at the battle of the Gates of Trajan near present-day Ihtiman, with Emperor Basil II barely escaping.

links.title: Battle of the Gates of Trajan

facts.text: The Scottish Reformation Parliament approved a Protestant confession of faith, initiating the Scottish Reformation and disestablishing Catholicism as the national religion.
Pike Place Market, one of the oldest continuously operated public farmers' markets in the U.S. and a popular tourist attraction, opened in Seattle, Washington.
Korean War: Forty-two American prisoners of war were massacred by the Korean People's Army on a hill above Waegwan, South Korea.
Michael Phelps won his eighth gold medal of the Summer Olympics in Beijing, setting the record for the most gold medals won by an athlete at a single games.
Second Fitna: Umayyad partisans defeated the supporters of Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr near Damascus, cementing Umayyad control of Syria.
Reconquista: After a four-month siege, the Catholic Monarchs of Spain conquered the city of Málaga from the Emirate of Granada.
John White, governor of the Roanoke Colony, the first English settlement in North America (located in present-day North Carolina ), returned after a three-year absence to find it deserted (depicted).
The trials of the Pendle and Samlesbury witches, among the most famous of England's witch trials, began at the assizes in Lancaster.
At least 9,000 enslaved people rebelled in the British colony in Demerara-Essequibo (in present-day Guyana), demanding emancipation.
American Civil War: At the Battle of Globe Tavern, Union forces attempted to sever the Weldon Railroad during the siege of Petersburg.
American astronomer Asaph Hall discovered Phobos, the larger of Mars's two moons, six days after discovering Deimos, the smaller one.
Russian Civil War: British motor torpedo boats raided the Bolshevik Baltic Fleet's home base of Kronstadt, sinking a depot ship and damaging a battleship.
A lightning strike started the Blackwater Fire in Shoshone National Forest, Wyoming, consuming 1,700 acres (7 km 2 ) of old-growth forest and killing 15 firefighters.

Second World War: During the Battle of Britain, the Luftwaffe made an all-out effort to destroy RAF Fighter Command, with both sides combined losing more aircraft on this day than at any other point during the campaign.
World War II: Amid a Soviet invasion of Japanese-held Sakhalin, Japanese police massacred 18 Koreans in Kamishisuka.
Australia won the fifth Test of the 1948 Ashes series, becoming the first Test cricket team to go undefeated in England, earning them the nickname "The Invincibles".

links.title: Australian cricket team in England in 1948

facts.text: East German Communist Party member Hildegard Trabant was killed while attempting to cross the Berlin Wall.
Hurricane Alicia made landfall near Galveston, Texas, causing $3 billion in damage and 21 fatalities.
Two people were fatally stabbed and eight others wounded by a rejected asylum seeker in an Islamist terrorist attack in Turku, Finland.
A meteor procession blazed across the night sky over Great Britain.
A hurricane struck the Caribbean island of Martinique, killing about 700 people, injuring at least 1,000 others, and causing severe damage.
The Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution was ratified, guaranteeing women's suffrage in the country.

links.title: Nineteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution
Women's suffrage in the United States

facts.text: Vietnam War: Members of the 6th Battalion of the Royal Australian Regiment were surrounded by a much larger Viet Cong unit at the Battle of Long Tan, but held them off for several hours until reinforcements arrived.
Pakistani president Pervez Musharraf resigned under pressure from a movement to impeach him.
Shortly after his return from the Ninth Crusade, Edward I was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey, nearly two years after his father 's death.
J. S. Bach led the first performance of Lobe den Herren, den mächtigen König der Ehren, BWV 137, a cantata setting the unchanged text of Neander's hymn.

links.title: Lobe den Herren, den mächtigen König der Ehren, BWV 137
Praise to the Lord, the Almighty

facts.text: Bonnie Prince Charlie raised the Jacobite standard at Glenfinnan, Scotland, in an attempt to regain the British throne for his father, beginning the Jacobite rising of 1745.
The Bersey Electric Cab entered service as the first electric taxi in London.
Russian Civil War: Peasants in Tambov Governorate began a rebellion against the Bolshevik government of Soviet Russia.
A referendum supported the recent merging of the posts of chancellor and president of Germany, consolidating Adolf Hitler 's assumption of supreme power.
A Hamas suicide bomber killed 23 people and wounded more than 130 others, including many Orthodox Jewish children, on a crowded public bus in Shmuel HaNavi, Jerusalem.
Thunderstorms in southern Ontario, Canada, spawned at least three tornadoes that caused over C$ 500 million in damage.

Seven Years' War: Having damaged several French vessels, British ships pursued the remainder of the fleet to Lagos, Portugal, and continued the battle there (depicted) in violation of Portuguese neutrality.
The 766th Independent Infantry Regiment of North Korea was disbanded after fighting for less than two months in the Korean War.
Second Chechen War: A Russian Mil Mi-26 was brought down by Chechen separatists with a man-portable air-defense system near Khankala, killing 127 people in the deadliest helicopter crash in history.
A car bomb destroyed the United Nations headquarters at Baghdad 's Canal Hotel, killing Brazilian diplomat Sérgio Vieira de Mello and 21 others.
Around 250,000 farmed non-native Atlantic salmon were accidentally released into the wild near Cypress Island, Washington.

links.title: Cypress Island Atlantic salmon pen break

facts.text: Byzantine–Bulgarian wars: Bulgarian forces led by Tsar Simeon I drove the Byzantines out of Thrace with a decisive victory at the Battle of Achelous.
The first Siege of Pensacola came to an end with the British and Creek abandoning their attempt to capture Pensacola in Spanish Florida.
Celtic Park, the largest football stadium in Scotland and home of Celtic F.C., opened.

links.title: List of football stadiums in Scotland

facts.text: Pluto was photographed for the first time at the Yerkes Observatory in Williams Bay, Wisconsin, U.S., 21 years before it was officially discovered by Clyde Tombaugh.

Hurricane-force winds combined hundreds of small fires in the U.S. states of Washington and Idaho into the Devil's Broom fire, which burned about 4,700 square miles (12,100 km²), the largest fire in recorded U.S. history.
Korean War: United Nations forces repelled an attempt by North Korea to capture the city of Taegu.
The Troubles: The Provisional Irish Republican Army bombed a bus carrying British Army soldiers in Northern Ireland, killing eight of them and wounding twenty-eight.
After colliding with the dredger Bowbelle on the River Thames in London, the pleasure boat Marchioness sank in thirty seconds, killing 51 people.
The Al-Shifa pharmaceutical factory in Sudan was destroyed by a missile attack launched by the United States in retaliation for the August 7 U.S. embassy bombings.

image.caption: Locations Khartoum , Sudan 15°38′45″N 32°33′42″E ﻿ / ﻿ 15.64583°N 32.56167°E ﻿ / 15.64583; 32.56167 Khost Province , Afghanistan

facts.text: Spanair Flight 5022 crashed just after take-off from Madrid's Barajas Airport, killing 154 people.
War of the Spanish Succession: A Spanish Bourbon army commanded by the Marquis de Bay was soundly defeated by a multinational army led by the Austrian commander Guido Starhemberg.
The American Professional Football Association, a predecessor of the National Football League, was founded.
Fires in the United States' Yellowstone National Park ravaged more than 150,000 acres (610 km 2 ) on the single worst day of the conflagration.

The final stage of the O-Bahn Busway in Adelaide, South Australia, was finished, completing at the time the world's longest and fastest guided busway, with buses travelling 12 km (7.5 mi) at speeds of up to 100 km/h (62 mph).

image.caption: A Custom Coaches CB80 bodied Scania K360UA on the O-Bahn Busway approaching Paradise Interchange

facts.text: Silent Sam, a Confederate monument on the campus of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was toppled by protestors.

links.title: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

facts.text: Jacobite clans clashed with a regiment of Covenanters in the streets of Dunkeld, Scotland.
Seventh Ottoman–Venetian War: Ottoman forces suddenly abandoned their siege of Corfu, allowing the Republic of Venice to preserve its rule over the Ionian Islands.
The national colours of Italy first appeared on a tricolour cockade in Genoa.
Leonardo da Vinci 's Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre by museum employee Vincenzo Peruggia and was not recovered until two years later.
World War II: A combined Canadian–Polish force captured the town of Falaise, France, in the final offensive of the Battle of Normandy.

American physicist Harry Daghlian accidentally dropped a tungsten carbide brick onto a plutonium bomb core, exposing himself to neutron radiation and later becoming the first Manhattan Project fatality due to a criticality accident.
Six people were killed during an escape attempt and riot at San Quentin State Prison in California; the subsequent trial of six inmates was the longest in state history at the time.
A limnic eruption of Lake Nyos in Cameroon released a cloud of carbon dioxide, suffocating 1,746 people and 3,500 livestock.
BioShock was released in North America, becoming a critical success and a demonstration of video games as an art form.

links.title: Video games as an art form

facts.text: Syrian civil war: Areas controlled by the Syrian opposition in Ghouta, Damascus, were attacked by rockets containing sarin, killing at least 281 people.
Austro-Turkish War: Austrian troops under Prince Eugene of Savoy captured the strategically important city of Belgrade from the Ottoman Empire.
Peninsular War: British and Portuguese forces put an end to the first French invasion of Portugal at the Battle of Vimeiro.
World War II: The Imperial Japanese Army lost the Battle of the Tenaru, the first of its three major land offensives during the Guadalcanal campaign.

South Vietnamese special forces loyal to Ngô Đình Nhu, the brother of President Ngô Đình Diệm, raided and vandalised Buddhist pagodas across the country, arresting thousands and leaving hundreds dead.

image.caption: Location Many Buddhist temples across South Vietnam , most notably the Xá Lợi Pagoda in Saigon

links.title: Army of the Republic of Vietnam Special Forces

facts.text: Passengers on a Thalys train from Amsterdam to Paris confronted and subdued an attacker who attempted a mass shooting.
The Vijayanagara Empire leased a small strip of land in present-day Chennai, the capital of the present-day Indian state of Tamil Nadu, to the East India Company.
King Charles I raised the royal standard at Nottingham, marking the beginning of the First English Civil War.
American Revolutionary War: Benedict Arnold used a ruse to convince the British that a much larger force was arriving, causing them to abandon the siege of Fort Stanwix.

image.caption: Date August 2–22, 1777 (2 weeks and 6 days) Location Fort Stanwix , New York 43°12′38″N 75°27′19″W ﻿ / ﻿ 43.21056°N 75.45528°W ﻿ / 43.21056; -75.45528 Result American victory

facts.text: Under the leadership of Henry Dunant and the International Committee of the Red Cross, twelve European states signed the First Geneva Convention, establishing rules for the protection of victims of armed conflict.

links.title: International Committee of the Red Cross

facts.text: First World War: German forces captured Rossignol in Belgium, taking more than 3,800 French prisoners.
First World War: A squadron of the 4th Royal Irish Dragoon Guards attacked a German scout party, the first engagement of British forces on the Western Front.
Ian Stephens, editor of The Statesman, defied British censorship to publish pictures of death and misery on Calcutta 's streets, informing the world of the Bengal famine of 1943.
An assassination attempt orchestrated by the OAS takes place against Charles de Gaulle, although he is uninjured.
The constitution of Singapore was amended to apportion seats to defeated opposition candidates in Parliament, which had hitherto entirely comprised members of the People's Action Party.
Grigori Perelman was awarded the Fields Medal for his proof of the Poincaré conjecture in mathematics but refused to accept the medal.
A series of ethnic clashes between the Orma and the Pokomo in Kenya's Tana River District resulted in at least 52 deaths.
A former military aircraft crashed at an airshow at Shoreham Airport in southern England, killing eleven people.
At the Battle of Bosworth Field, Lancastrian forces under Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, defeated Yorkist forces under Richard III of England, decisively ending the Wars of the Roses.
Queen Anne's War: A British attempt to attack Quebec failed when eight ships wrecked on the St. Lawrence River.
The yacht America won the race for the Cup of One Hundred Sovereigns, later renamed the America's Cup, near the Isle of Wight, England.
A fire broke out on British Airtours Flight 28M at Manchester Airport, causing 55 deaths mostly due to smoke inhalation, and leading to changes to make aircraft evacuation more effective.

Roy Moore, Alabama's chief justice, was suspended after refusing to comply with a U.S. federal court order to remove a rock inscribed with the Ten Commandments from the lobby of the Supreme Court of Alabama building.
The Albert Bridge, spanning the River Thames in London, opened to traffic.
The Southern Cross Expedition, the first British venture of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration, departed London.
In their first major action of the First World War, the British Expeditionary Force engaged German troops in Mons, Belgium.
The Chesapeake–Potomac hurricane made landfall in the Outer Banks of North Carolina and went on to cause at least 47 deaths in the U.S. Mid-Atlantic region.

Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union signed the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, a ten-year mutual non-aggression treaty, which also secretly divided northern and eastern Europe into German and Soviet spheres of influence.
Second World War: A decisive Soviet victory against German forces at the Battle of Kursk gave the Red Army the strategic initiative for the rest of the war.
The Cruise of the Kings, a royal cruise organised by the Queen Consort of Greece, Frederica of Hanover, departed from Marseille, France.

Singing Revolution: Approximately two million people joined hands to form a human chain spanning 675.5 kilometres (419.7 mi) across the Estonian, Latvian and Lithuanian Soviet republics to demonstrate their desire for independence.
The World Wide Web was opened to the public.
William Wallace, a leader of Scottish resistance against England during the Wars of Scottish Independence, was hanged, drawn and quartered.
King George III issued a proclamation that declared elements of the American colonies of Great Britain to be in a state of "open and avowed rebellion".
Congo Crisis: In order to stop the secession of South Kasai from the Republic of Congo, Armée Nationale Congolaise forces launched an invasion of South Kasai.

links.title: Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo

facts.text: Natascha Kampusch, who had been abducted at the age of ten in Vienna, escaped from her captor's house in Strasshof an der Nordbahn after more than eight years in captivity.
A 5.8 M W earthquake struck the Piedmont region of Virginia, and was felt by more people than any other quake in U.S. history.
89 New Zealand Native football team
Rome was sacked for the first time in approximately 800 years by the Visigoths under Alaric I.
A Dutch expedition arrived at the mouth of the Valdivia River, in present-day Chile, to establish a new colony in the ruins of the abandoned Spanish settlement of Valdivia.
The 1662 Book of Common Prayer was legally enforced as the liturgy of the Church of England, precipitating the Great Ejection of Dissenter ministers from their benefices.
War of the Spanish Succession: An Anglo-Dutch fleet engaged a French naval force at the Battle of Málaga in the Mediterranean Sea.
War of 1812: British forces invaded Washington, D.C., setting fire to various U.S. government buildings, including the White House.

image.caption: Date August 24, 1814 Location Washington, D.C. 38°53′23″N 77°00′32″W ﻿ / ﻿ 38.88972°N 77.00889°W ﻿ / 38.88972; -77.00889 Result British victory

facts.text: The New Zealand Native football team, predominantly comprising Māori players, concluded their 107-game tour, the longest in rugby union history.
The Battle of Cer ended with the first Allied victory of World War I.
The Royal Navy 's R.38, the world's largest airship at the time, was destroyed by a structural failure over Hull, killing 44 of the 49 crew aboard.

World War II: At the Battle of the Eastern Solomons, bombers from the U.S. aircraft carrier Saratoga sank the Japanese aircraft carrier Ryūjō near Santa Isabel Island, contributing to an Allied victory.
In the midst of a political crisis, Brazilian president Getúlio Vargas fatally shot himself in the Catete Palace in Rio de Janeiro.

Buddhist crisis: The U.S. State Department ordered Ambassador Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. to encourage South Vietnamese Army officers to oust Ngo Dinh Diem if he did not willingly remove Ngo Dinh Nhu from his unofficial position of power.

links.title: Army of the Republic of Vietnam

facts.text: Hurricane Andrew, the third-most intense Category 5 cyclone to impact the United States in the 20th century, made landfall in southern Florida.
The International Astronomical Union passed a resolution redefining the term planet and classifying Pluto as a dwarf planet.
The oldest known version of the Gutenberg Bible, the first major book produced on a printing press, was completed.
American Revolutionary War: Near present-day Aurora, Indiana, American Indians led by Joseph Brant killed or captured all members of a Pennsylvania militia.
The New York City branch of the Ohio Life Insurance and Trust Co. collapsed following widespread embezzlement, leading to a severe recession that caused about 5,000 businesses to fail.

links.title: Ohio Life Insurance and Trust Company

facts.text: Adolf Hitler ordered the suspension of the T4 euthanasia program of the mentally ill and disabled, although killings continued in secret for the remainder of World War II.
Cultural Revolution: Red Guards vandalised the Jokhang (depicted), the holiest Buddhist temple in Tibet.
George Mouzalon, the regent of the Empire of Nicaea, was assassinated as part of a conspiracy led by nobles under the future emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos.
The Honourable Artillery Company, now the oldest surviving regiment in the British Army, was granted a royal charter by Henry VIII.
Seven Years' War: Prussian forces engaged the Russians at the Battle of Zorndorf in present-day Sarbinowo, Poland.
World War I: During the sack of Louvain in Belgium, German troops burned the town's Catholic university, destroying several medieval manuscripts.
Bruce Springsteen released his commercial breakthrough album, Born to Run.
The NASA spacecraft Voyager 2 made its closest approach to Neptune and provided definitive proof of the existence of the planet's rings.
American singer Aaliyah and several members of her record company were killed when their overloaded aircraft crashed shortly after takeoff from Marsh Harbour Airport in The Bahamas.

image.caption: Born Aaliyah Dana Haughton ( 1979-01-16 ) January 16, 1979 New York City, US

facts.text: Mexican drug war: Fifty-two people were killed in an arson attack at a casino in Monterrey, Mexico.
The NASA space probe Voyager 1 became the first man-made object to enter interstellar space.
Philip III became King of France following the death of his father Louis IX during the Eighth Crusade.
Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei demonstrated his first telescope to Venetian lawmakers.

image.caption: Born Galileo di Vincenzo Bonaiuti de' Galilei [ 1 ] ( 1564-02-15 ) 15 February 1564 [ 2 ] Pisa , Florence

facts.text: Matthew Webb became the first person to swim across the English Channel, doing so in approximately 21 hours 40 minutes.

links.title: List of successful English Channel swimmers

facts.text: World War II: Japanese forces attacked the Australian base at Milne Bay on the eastern tip of New Guinea.
The skeleton of King Richard III of England was discovered under a car park in Leicester.

links.title: Exhumation and reburial of Richard III of England

facts.text: Second Fitna: The Battle of al-Harra was fought between Umayyad forces and the rebel defenders of Medina at a lava field northeast of the city.
Byzantine–Seljuk wars: Seljuk Turks led by Alp Arslan captured Byzantine emperor Romanos IV at the Battle of Manzikert.
The first Lutheran denomination in North America, the Pennsylvania Ministerium, was founded in Philadelphia.
French Revolution: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, defining a set of individual and collective rights of the people, was approved by the National Constituent Assembly.

links.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

facts.text: World War I: The German colony of Togoland surrendered to French and British forces after a 20-day campaign.

World War I: As the British Expeditionary Force and French Fifth Army began their retreat from Mons, the British II Corps delayed the pursuing Germans at the Battle of Le Cateau long enough for the main force to escape.
At a cafe in Paisley, Scotland, a woman found the remains of a snail in her bottle of ginger beer, giving rise to the landmark civil action case Donoghue v Stevenson.
The 1940 New England hurricane formed over the Atlantic Ocean; it would go on to cause widespread damage despite never making landfall in the United States.
The Coatzacoalcos earthquake struck near the Mexican state of Veracruz, killing 25 people.
The South African Defence Force launched an attack against SWAPO guerrilla fighters at Omugulugwombashe, starting the South African Border War.
The Beatles released " Hey Jude ", which became the then-longest single to top the UK charts.
The U.S. Democratic Party 's National Convention opened in Chicago, sparking four days of clashes between anti-Vietnam War protesters and police.

links.title: Opposition to United States involvement in the Vietnam War

facts.text: Betty Friedan and the National Organization for Women organized the Women's Strike for Equality in New York City, in which 50,000 women protested the continuing lack of gender equality.
A bomb was planted at Harvey's Resort Hotel in Stateline, Nevada, which the FBI later described as the most complex improvised explosive device ever created.
After a ceasefire was reached in the Russo-Georgian War, Russia recognized the independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

links.title: International recognition of Abkhazia and South Ossetia

facts.text: Hundred Years' War: At the Battle of Crécy, English forces established the military supremacy of English longbows over the French combination of crossbows and armoured knights.
Quincy Market in Boston opens as a replacement for an overcrowded market in Faneuil Hall, later becoming a major tourist attraction.
A massive eruption destroyed the island of Krakatoa, Indonesia, ejecting so much volcanic ash that average global temperatures fell by as much as 1.2 °C (2.2 °F) over the next year.
Pather Panchali, the first film in The Apu Trilogy by Satyajit Ray, was released and went on to win many Indian and international film awards.
Two American journalists were murdered on live television while conducting an interview in Moneta, Virginia.

links.title: Murders of Alison Parker and Adam Ward

facts.text: The sacking of Rome by the Visigoths ended after three days.
In the shortest recorded war in history, the Sultanate of Zanzibar surrendered to the United Kingdom after less than an hour of conflict.
The first edition of the Guinness Book of Records was published.

South Vietnamese junta leader Nguyễn Khánh entered into a triumvirate power-sharing arrangement with rival generals Trần Thiện Khiêm and Dương Văn Minh, both of whom had been involved in plots to unseat Khánh.

Comair Flight 5191 crashed while inadvertently attempting to take off from the wrong runway at Blue Grass Airport in Lexington, Kentucky, killing 49 of the 50 people on board, and causing the Federal Aviation Administration to modify air traffic control rules.
The Myanmar military junta and ethnic armies began three days of violent clashes in the region of Kokang.
British forces led by William Howe defeated the Continental Army under George Washington at the Battle of Long Island, the largest battle of the American Revolutionary War.
Napoleonic Wars: The French Navy defeated the Royal Navy, preventing them from capturing the harbour of Grand Port on Mauritius.
Black Hawk, the leader of the Sauk tribe of Native Americans, surrendered to U.S. authorities to end the Black Hawk War.

image.caption: Born c. 1767 Saukenuk , Illinois Country , British America

links.title: Native Americans in the United States

facts.text: The Troubles: the IRA ambushed and killed 18 British soldiers near Warrenpoint, and assassinated Lord Mountbatten on his boat at Mullaghmore.
American musician Stevie Ray Vaughan, one of the most influential guitarists in the revival of blues in the 1980s, was killed in a helicopter crash.
Ottoman–Portuguese conflicts: During the Battle of Wofla, the Portuguese commander Cristóvão da Gama was captured by the Adal Sultanate and executed the next day.
Ferdinand II, King of Bohemia and Hungary, was unanimously elected Holy Roman Emperor.
Bishops' Wars: Scottish Covenanter forces led by Alexander Leslie defeated the English army near Newburn, England.
William Herschel discovered Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, during the first use of his new telescope which was then the largest in the world.

links.title: List of largest optical telescopes historically

facts.text: The 1909 Monterrey hurricane dissipated; one of the deadliest Atlantic tropical cyclones on record, it killed an estimated 4,000 people throughout Mexico.
A confrontation at Blargies prison camp in France led to a charge of mutiny for New Zealand private John Braithwaite, for which he was later executed.

American civil-rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. delivered the speech " I Have a Dream " during the March on Washington, calling for civil and economic rights and an end to racism in the United States.

links.title: March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom

facts.text: Construction began on the Ryugyong Hotel in Pyongyang, the tallest building in North Korea.

image.caption: Interactive map of the Ryugyong Hotel area

links.title: List of tallest buildings in North Korea

facts.text: The NASA spacecraft Galileo flew by the asteroid 243 Ida and took photographs that later revealed the first known asteroid moon.
The second phase of the Thomson-East Coast MRT line was opened for service.
A mass shooting took place in Phoenix, Arizona, leaving 33 dead and five others injured.
Orestes took control of Ravenna, the capital of the Western Roman Empire, forcing Emperor Julius Nepos to flee.
Tom Thumb, the first American-built steam locomotive, took part in an impromptu race against a horse-drawn car in Maryland.

image.caption: Type and origin Power type Steam Builder Peter Cooper Build date 1829 ; 197 years ago ( 1829 )

facts.text: American tennis player Althea Gibson became the first African-American woman to compete at the U.S. National Championships.
African-American teenager Emmett Till was lynched near Money, Mississippi, for allegedly flirting with a white woman, energizing the nascent American civil rights movement.
Swedish police used gas bombs to end a seven-day hostage situation in Stockholm; the hostages had bonded with their captors during the incident, leading to the term Stockholm syndrome.
Hundred Years' War: Led by King Edward III, a fleet of 50 English ships captured at least 14 Castilian vessels and sank several more at the Battle of Winchelsea.
Angered by high tax burdens and disfranchisement, farmers in western Massachusetts led by Daniel Shays began an armed uprising against the U.S. federal government.
Michael Faraday first experimentally demonstrated electromagnetic induction, leading to the formulation of the law of induction named after him.

image.caption: Born ( 1791-09-22 ) 22 September 1791 Newington Butts , Surrey , England

facts.text: Under the Treaty of Nanking, an " unequal treaty " that ended the First Opium War, the Chinese island from which Hong Kong would grow was ceded to Britain.
Slava, the last of five Borodino -class battleships, was launched by the Imperial Russian Navy.
Due to price increases on macaroni products, rioting occurred in the Little Italy area of Providence, Rhode Island.
Congress passed the Philippine Autonomy Act, the first formal and official declaration of the U.S.'s commitment to grant independence to the Philippines.
The Soviet Union conducted its first nuclear weapons test, detonating the 22- kiloton RDS-1.

links.title: List of nuclear weapons tests of the Soviet Union

facts.text: Followers of Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh began deliberately infecting people in The Dalles, Oregon, with Salmonella in the first and largest bioterrorist attack in United States history.
Italian businessman Libero Grassi was killed by the Sicilian Mafia in Palermo after taking a public stand against their extortion demands.
Vnukovo Airlines Flight 2801 crashed on approach to Svalbard Airport, Norway, killing all 141 on board.
Six nuclear warheads were mistakenly loaded onto a United States Air Force heavy bomber that flew from Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana.

links.title: 2007 United States Air Force nuclear weapons incident

facts.text: Chen Quanguo became the Chinese Communist Party secretary of Xinjiang, and in that role later oversaw the creation of the Xinjiang internment camps.
France signed the Treaty of Picquigny with England, freeing Louis XI to deal with the threat posed by Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy.
Gottlieb Daimler patented the world's first internal-combustion motorcycle, the Reitwagen.

image.caption: Manufacturer Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach

facts.text: The last member of the Yahi, known as Ishi, emerged from the wilderness near Oroville, California, to join European American society.
Mona Best opened the Casbah Coffee Club with a performance by the Quarrymen, the precursor of the Beatles.
Air France Flight 343 crashed while attempting to land at Yoff Airport, Dakar, killing all 63 occupants.
Guru Ram Das became the fourth of the Sikh gurus, the spiritual masters of Sikhism.
King James VI of Scotland held a masque at the baptism of Prince Henry, his first child.

links.title: Masque at the baptism of Prince Henry

facts.text: World War I: The Battle of Tannenberg resulted in the almost complete destruction of the Russian 2nd Army by the German 8th Army.
British and Australian prisoners of war in Singapore revolted against their Japanese captors, who required them to pledge not to escape.
Second World War: German field marshal Erwin Rommel launched the last major Axis offensive of the Western Desert campaign, attacking British positions near El Alamein, Egypt.
South Vietnamese opposition figure Phan Quang Đán was elected to the National Assembly, despite soldiers being bussed in to vote multiple times for President Ngô Đình Diệm 's candidate.
Writer and politician Abdul Muis became the first person to be awarded the posthumous title of National Hero of Indonesia.
An express train carrying foreign workers from Yugoslavia to West Germany derailed in Zagreb, killing 153 people.
Iranian president Mohammad-Ali Rajai and prime minister Mohammad-Javad Bahonar were assassinated in a bombing committed by the People's Mojahedin Organization of Iran.
Discovery, the third orbiter of NASA 's Space Shuttle program, lifted off on its maiden voyage from Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
Gulf War: US General Norman Schwarzkopf Jr. issued General Order No. 1 prohibiting US troops from consuming alcohol or possessing pornographic material.
A heavy bomber that had been unintentionally loaded with nuclear missiles flew them from North Dakota to Louisiana before they were recognized.

links.title: 2007 United States Air Force nuclear weapons incident

facts.text: Ukrainian politician Andriy Parubiy was assassinated in Lviv, Ukraine.
Paul II succeeded Pius II as pope of the Catholic Church.
European settlers landing on the north banks of the Yarra River in Southeastern Australia founded the city of Melbourne.

image.caption: Melbourne Show map of Australia Melbourne Show map of Victoria Melbourne Show map of Oceania

facts.text: Thurgood Marshall was confirmed as the first African-American Supreme Court justice.

links.title: Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States

facts.text: A powerful bomb exploded at the Mitsubishi Heavy Industries headquarters in Marunouchi, Tokyo, killing eight people.
The last remaining American troops left Afghanistan, ending U.S. involvement in the war.
Al-Kamil became the fourth sultan of the Ayyubid dynasty of Egypt.
The body of Mary Ann Nichols, the alleged first victim of an unidentified serial killer known as Jack the Ripper, was found in Buck's Row, London.
Thomas Edison was granted a patent for the Kinetoscope, a precursor to the modern movie projector.
Second World War: Two Royal navy destroyers were lost to mines and two other vessels damaged off Texel, Netherlands, killing around 300 men.
World War II: A detachment of Chetniks captured the town of Loznica in German-occupied Serbia.

links.title: Territory of the Military Commander in Serbia

facts.text: The Matagorda hurricane, the most intense and costliest tropical cyclone of the 1942 Atlantic hurricane season, dissipated after causing $26.5 million in damages and eight deaths.
On the final day of the Isle of Wight Festival 1969, attended by approximately 150,000 people over three days, Bob Dylan appeared in his first gig in three years.
Diana, Princess of Wales, her partner Dodi Fayed, and their driver were killed in a car crash in Paris.

links.title: Death of Diana, Princess of Wales

facts.text: Typhoon Rusa made landfall in Goheung as the most powerful typhoon to hit South Korea in 43 years, killing at least 236 people.
A sightseeing helicopter crashed in the mountains of Skoddevarre in Alta, Norway, killing all six people on board.
War of 1812: American militia forces repelled a British force at the Battle of Caulk's Field, killing 41 people including Captain Peter Parker of the Royal Navy.
Sultan Murad V of the Ottoman Empire was deposed after a reign of 93 days on grounds of mental illness.
Nazi forces, posing as Poles, staged an attack against the German radio station Sender Gleiwitz in Gleiwitz, Upper Silesia, Germany, creating an excuse to invade Poland the next day.
A parcel bomb sent by Ngô Đình Nhu, younger brother and chief adviser of South Vietnamese president Ngô Đình Diệm, failed to kill Norodom Sihanouk, Prime Minister of Cambodia.
The last episode of The Bill, the longest-running police drama in British television history, was broadcast.
